subject: Vector/matrix assignments in an NMF model

messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Vector/matrix assignments in an NMF model
parts:
Hi all,

Here's a Stan model of non-negative matrix factorisation (actually a
bit PLCA-style) intended as a simple model of the type used for music
transcription:
https://gist.github.com/danstowell/151a3b68ceb9c5f4a51f

It works fine on small toy data. I'd just like to ask if the example
could be written better because I ended up doing a couple of inelegant
things:
* flipping the matrix "Wmat" since it seemed I could directly assign a
simplex into a matrix row not into a matrix column;
* iterating over the columns of a matrix to specify them all as
exponential rather than writing a single "~ exponential()" for the
whole lot.

There might be a neater way that I've missed.

Thanks
Dan
--
http://www.mcld.co.uk

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vector/matrix assignments in an NMF model
parts:
Thanks for sharing the model. In terms of the model,
what's the motivation for flattening Xnorm and using
a single Dirichlet rather than doing it column or row-wise?

For efficiency:

1. calculate Xnorm, Wmat and Winitnorm in the transformed
data block. From what I can tell, they only depend on data.
Then they'll only be calculated once rather than potentially
several times per iteration. Then all the transposing and
what not is only done once so nothing at all to worry about for
speed.

2. Rather than iterating over columns a matrix, you can
just do:

to_vector(H) ~ exponential(Hconc);

We're working on making more direct implementations for this,
but this is the best that's available now.

- Bob

messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vector/matrix assignments in an NMF model
parts:
Bob,

Thanks. I had thought of your suggestion 2, on the assumption that
to_vector() is low-cost because essentially a "static cast" (talking
in C terminology), but decided not to make C-like assumptions... I
wonder how users can be confident about which are the expensive and
cheap operations? Experience I guess.

Regarding the Dirichlet choice: in my reading of PLCA the entire
observed spectrogram is treated as if it represented samples from a
big multinomial, though that multinomial itself factorises along rows
and columns. No?
(BTW in my code I chose to model it as a multinomial sampled from some
dirichlet, rather than some quanta sampled from a multinomial.)

Best
Dan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vector/matrix assignments in an NMF model
parts:
Like all programming, writing efficient Stan programs
comes down to understanding how they get compiled and executed.

There's a discussion in the arrays and matrices chapter of
the manual that tries to explain those decisions.

There's also a discussion of how code in different blocks
gets executed and when.

The big picture for Stan (both MCMC and optimization)
is that taking gradients is expensive compared
to everything else. Doing work on simple data types like
vectors is usually a win if it cuts down on work done for
gradients. So basically anything that can be done to vectorize
a sampling statement (or a function evaluation like normal_log)
is a win. In the best case, fewer calculations will be done
such as log(sigma) in normal_log(y,mu,sigma) if y and/or mu
are vectors.

Unlike in R or Python, loops themselves aren't the expensive part.
Only when they prevent vectorization of probability functions or
other derivative-involving operations.

- Bob
